Received 7 December 2024 l Revised 28 January 2025 l Accepted 17 February 2025 l Published online 17 June 2025 Abstract: Objective: To evaluate the effects of a blended aqueous extract of Moringa oleifera, Ocimum gratissimum, and Vernonia amygdalina on some markers of thromboinflammation in diabetic rats. Material and Methods: We administered 150 mg/kg body weight of the individual extracts and the blended extract (1:1:1) to diabetic induced rats for 28 days. Acute toxicity of the extracts were determined by the Lorke technique while the markers of thromboinflammation, involving platelet count, mean platelet volume, platelet distribution width, plateletcrit, platelet large cell ratio, absolute white blood cell, lymphocytes, neutrophils, monocytes, basophils and eosinophils, were determined as part of the complete blood count using an automated hematology analyzer. Results: The LD50 of both the individual and blended extracts were observed to be above 5,000 mg/kg body weight. There was a significant increase in the serum glucose and markers of thromboinflammation involving the total white blood cell count, neutrophil count, platelet count, plateletcrit, mean platelet volume, platelet distribution width and the platelet large cell ratio, but a decrease in the lymphocyte and eosinophil count for the diabetic non-extract treated rats. The diabetic rats treated with the blended extract showed a significant restoration of the parameters. Conclusion: This study revealed that the blended aqueous extracts of Moringa oleifera, Ocimum gratissimum, and Vernonia amygdalina are non-toxic and may have synergistic effects in limiting thromboinflammation in a diabetic state. JSON: Name: triherbal_anti_thromboinflammation Title: In vivo hematological assessment of anti-thromboinflammatory effects of a blended aqueous extract of Moringa oleifera, Ocimum gratissimum, and Vernonia amygdalina in alloxan-induced diabetic rats Short Hypothesis: Oral administration of a 1:1:1 blended aqueous extract of Moringa oleifera, Ocimum gratissimum, and Vernonia amygdalina at 150 mg/kg for 28 days reduces thromboinflammatory markers (platelet count, MPV, PDW, PCT, P-LCR, total WBC and neutrophil counts) and lowers serum glucose in alloxan-induced diabetic rats compared with untreated diabetic controls. Related Work: Prior preclinical work reports antidiabetic, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities for individual aqueous extracts of Moringa oleifera, Ocimum gratissimum and Vernonia amygdalina; separate studies have measured hematological endpoints and showed extract-associated changes in glycemia and some blood parameters. Polyherbal and blended preparations have been used empirically and a few studies report hypoglycemic effects for combinations, but existing work lacks standardized, quantitative comparisons of blended versus individual extracts on a comprehensive panel of thromboinflammation biomarkers. Reported limitations in the literature include small group sizes, inconsistent extract preparation and phytochemical standardization, absence of dose–response characterization, limited thrombosis-relevant endpoints (often only glucose or a single CBC parameter), and scarce data on coagulation, platelet function, inflammatory cytokines, oxidative stress, or histopathology. Mechanistic links between glycemic control and direct antithrombotic effects remain unresolved. Abstract: Thromboinflammation contributes to diabetes complications but preclinical evidence for multi-herbal interventions against thromboinflammatory dysregulation is limited. This study proposes a controlled in vivo evaluation of a blended aqueous extract (1:1:1) of Moringa oleifera, Ocimum gratissimum and Vernonia amygdalina in an alloxan-induced rat model of diabetes. Using standardized extract preparation and quantitative phytochemical profiling, treated and control groups will be compared over 28 days for primary hematological thromboinflammation markers (platelet count, MPV, PDW, PCT, P-LCR, total WBC and neutrophils) and secondary endpoints (serum glucose, PT/aPTT, D-dimer, IL-6, TNF-α, oxidative stress markers, and vascular/pancreatic histopathology). The main contribution is a structured, dose‐response and comparative assessment of blended versus individual extracts with matched positive (metformin) and negative controls, enabling attribution of effects to the blend. Expected outcomes are demonstration of dose-dependent reduction in thromboinflammatory markers and improved glycemic control with the blended extract, providing preclinical evidence to justify mechanistic studies and translational evaluation. Experiments: Model and animals: Male Wistar rats, 8–10 weeks, randomized. Sample size: n=10 per group (power 0.8, α=0.05 to detect ≥30% change in primary endpoints). Diabetes induction: alloxan monohydrate 20 mg/kg i.p. daily for 2 days as per source protocol; confirm diabetes by random blood glucose (RBG) >200 mg/dL at 72 h. Treatment arms (28 days): G1: non-diabetic vehicle control; G2: diabetic vehicle control; G3: diabetic + metformin 40 mg/kg (positive control); G4: diabetic + MOAE 150 mg/kg; G5: diabetic + OGAE 150 mg/kg; G6: diabetic + VAAE 150 mg/kg; G7: diabetic + blended extract (1:1:1) 150 mg/kg; G8–G9: blended extract dose-response (50 mg/kg and 300 mg/kg). Additional acute toxicity arm: confirm LD50 >5000 mg/kg via Lorke method. Extract preparation: aqueous decoction, yield recorded, batch HPLC phytochemical quantification (flavonoids, alkaloids, tannins, saponins, terpenoids, phenols). Timepoints: baseline (pre-induction), day 3 (post-induction), weekly (days 7, 14, 21), terminal (day 28). Primary endpoints: CBC by automated hematology analyzer — platelet count, MPV, PDW, PCT, P-LCR, total WBC, neutrophil %, lymphocyte %. Secondary endpoints: RBG, fasting glucose, PT, aPTT, plasma D-dimer, ex vivo platelet aggregation (ADP and collagen agonists) using PRP, inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-α) by ELISA, oxidative stress markers (MDA, SOD activity), histopathology of pancreas and mesenteric/arterial endothelium and immunohistochemistry for endothelial activation (VCAM-1, ICAM-1). Data handling: report absolute values and % change from baseline. Statistical analysis: one-way ANOVA with Tukey post-hoc for group comparisons; repeated measures ANOVA for time series; two-sided p<0.05 significant. Comparisons and ablations: blended extract vs each individual extract and vs metformin; dose-response across blended doses; correlation analysis between glucose change and thromboinflammation markers; sensitivity analysis excluding animals with incomplete diabetes induction. Outcome metrics: mean difference and 95% CI for primary endpoints, effect sizes (Cohen's d), and adjusted p-values for multiple comparisons. Risk Factors and Limitations: Variability and reproducibility: aqueous extract composition may vary with plant source, harvest time and preparation method, limiting reproducibility and comparability. Model limitations: alloxan-induced diabetes models predominantly beta-cell cytotoxicity and may not model type 2 diabetes pathophysiology or chronic metabolic inflammation. Attribution ambiguity: reductions in thromboinflammatory markers may result indirectly from glycemic lowering rather than direct anti-thrombotic actions; distinguishing mechanisms requires additional targeted assays. Biomarker constraints: CBC and coagulation assays are surrogate measures and may not capture thrombotic risk fully; lack of in vivo thrombosis functional endpoints (e.g., arterial thrombosis models) limits translational inference. Statistical and power risks: effect size assumptions may be optimistic; underpowered groups will yield inconclusive results. Ethical and resource constraints: performing comprehensive cytokine, aggregation, and histopathology assays increases cost and may limit sample sizes. Translation: rodent hematology and platelet biology differ from humans, constraining direct clinical extrapolation. Analytical confounders: hemolysis, platelet clumping, or assay variability can bias hematology results. Safety scope: LD50 does not replace chronic toxicity, pharmacokinetics or interaction profiling required for translational development.
